verses.translation_literal: Of David. A psalm. Utterance of YHWH to my lord: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song of David. And now a voice breaks the silence, and it is the voice of the LORD himself, speaking to one whom the singer calls my lord: Sit. Sit at my right hand, in the place of honour and of strength, and wait, until I have made your enemies a footstool beneath your feet.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play this as a court scene, not a vision. The heading says 'of David', and the little word lamed can mean 'by', 'for' or 'about'. That range is plain Hebrew grammar. Radak, who reads the psalm as about David, takes the lamed as 'for David', comparing 'say of me: he is my brother' (Gen 20:13, where lamed means 'of me'). Ibn Ezra holds that another poet composed the psalm about David, and he sets its writing at the time David's men swore he should not go out with them to war. So the singer who says 'my lord' is a court poet speaking of the king, and the actor must decide where the poet stands in the room: below the throne, looking up.

The KJV's 'The Lord said unto my Lord' hides the Hebrew in capital letters. The first is YHWH, the covenant name. The second is adoni, 'my lord', the ordinary word for a master or king, never used of God with this suffix. The KJV also softens נְאֻם: it is not the plain verb 'said' but the oracle formula of the prophets, 'utterance of', a solemn announcement. Make the pause after it long. Sitting at the right hand is the posture of a royal deputy and co-ruler: the right hand is the hand of action and protection. A footstool (hadom) is a real piece of throne furniture. Egyptian and Near Eastern reliefs show kings with captives' bodies or heads under their feet. Rashi and the Targum bring the verse's setting differently (Abraham and the four kings, or David waiting for Saul); the stage picture is the same: sit, and wait for the LORD to act.

philological_notes.note: The lamed of the heading can mean 'of', 'by', 'for' or 'about': that is general grammar. Radak takes it as 'for David', comparing Gen 20:13. Ibn Ezra reads the psalm as written about David by another poet.
The oracle formula: a solemn 'utterance of', most often heard in the prophets. It marks what follows as a declaration from God, not an ordinary remark.
'To my lord', with the pointing -ֹנִי used for human lords; the divine title would be pointed אֲדֹנָי. The speaker is therefore not addressing God but the one set beside him.
A footstool, the low support in front of a throne. Metzudat Zion defines it as the stool under the seated person's feet, comparing 'they worshipped at his footstool' (Ps 99).

verses.translation_literal: The staff of your strength YHWH will send out from Zion: rule in the midst of your enemies.
verses.translation_dramatic: From Zion the LORD will stretch out the staff of your strength, and it is his hand that sends it. And now, rule. Rule, right there in the middle of your enemies.
verses.directors_commentary:
Hebrew puts the object first: 'The staff of your strength' leads the line, then the verb, then the LORD, then Zion. The sentence is built to put the king's own sceptre in the first place and God as the one who sends it. The KJV's 'rod' is fine, but 'rod of thy strength' reads as a bare ornament; מַטֶּה is both the royal sceptre and the shepherd's or soldier's staff, the thing a commander leans on and strikes with. Rashi relates it to מַשְׁעֵן, 'support' (compare 'the whole staff of bread' in Psalm 105:16), and Metzudat David paraphrases 'the support of your strength'. So the staff is the king's power itself, which comes from God, not from the king.

Zion is the stronghold David took, according to Radak, at the start of his reign, and the seat of the ark, so authority 'goes out' from it as from a capital. The verb שָׁלַח, 'send, stretch out', is the verb used of a hand sent out; the staff is extended like an arm.

The last words are the shock. רְדֵה is the imperative of רָדָה, 'to rule, to tread down', the same root as the verb used for humankind's dominion in Genesis 1:26, and also for treading grapes (Joel 4:13), so it carries an edge of trampling. And it is 'in the midst of' (בְּקֶרֶב) enemies: the king rules while surrounded. Radak points out that this does not mean only the neighbouring Philistine towns; it means in the very heart of their land. The KJV 'rule thou in the midst of thine enemies' is accurate here and the performer should play the line as a command from a safe place to a king standing where the danger is.

philological_notes.note: A staff, rod, or tribal sceptre. Rashi takes it as 'support' (Psalm 105:16); Meiri reads it as the sceptre of kingship, recalling Genesis 49:10.
'Rule' or 'tread down'; Metzudat Zion links it to 'he shall rule from sea to sea' (Psalm 72:8).

verses.translation_literal: Your people [are] freewill offerings on the day of your strength, in holy splendours, from the womb of dawn; yours [is] the dew of your youth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your people come to you, and no one has called them. They are freewill offerings, given gladly, on the day your strength is summoned. They come in holy splendour, out of the womb of the dawn itself, and the dew of your youth is yours, fresh as the first light.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the verse where the English versions fall apart, and the actor should know why. The first clause has no verb. 'Your people' are freewill offerings (nedavot): the people do not merely volunteer, they are the gift. Ibn Ezra reads the plural as shorthand, like 'a rain of freewill offerings' (Ps 68:10), and takes it to say that if war is needed, your people will come to you freely. The KJV's 'shall be willing in the day of thy power' turns the noun into a verb and adds a future; 'power' for chayil also loses the sense of an army and its muster, which is what 'strength' means in the day of battle. Rashi and Metzudat David tie the volunteers to Abraham's allies, Aner, Eshkol and Mamre. In the staging, picture men coming without conscription or pay.

Then the images pile up with no grammar to join them: 'in holy splendours, from the womb of dawn'. The KJV's 'beauties of holiness' and the ASV's 'holy array' both smooth over how strange 'womb of dawn' is. Dawn has a womb, and out of it comes the dew. The Hebrew word for dawn, mishchar, appears nowhere else in the Bible, so every reading is a guess: Ibn Ezra lists several, including 'from dawn's rising' (reading the dew as the volunteers coming at first light), and Rashi takes the 'womb' as the moment of birth. Metzudat Zion links it to the root of 'seeking' (Job 24:5), which gives 'from the dawn of seeking you'. Dew is the picture of something that comes silently, in great numbers, at the start of the day, and cannot be commanded. The last words, 'the dew of your youth', add that this freshness belongs to the addressee himself.

philological_notes.note: Freewill offerings: gifts given not because a law requires them. The sentence has no verb, so the people are called the offerings, not just willing. Ibn Ezra reads it as shorthand for 'like a rain of freewill offerings'.

Plural construct of hadar, 'splendour, majesty': 'in splendours of holiness'. Radak reads the plural as 'beautiful in many ways' and the place as Jerusalem; Metzudat David reads it as a reward for the king's own holiness. English versions vary between 'beauties', 'array' and 'honours'.

A word found only here in the Bible, presumably 'dawn' (shachar) with a prefix mem. Metzudat Zion links it to the root of seeking, as in Job 24:5. The phrase 'womb of dawn' is a bold metaphor, not a technical term.

'Your youth': a singular noun that carries the suffix -ֶיךָ, which usually marks plural nouns. This is my own description of the form, with no source. Rashi's citations spell the word both ways: יַלְדוּתֶיךָ in the lemma, and in his second reading יַלְדוּתֶךָ.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH has sworn, and he will not relent: You [are] a priest for ever, upon the matter of Melchizedek.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD has sworn, and he does not take it back. Hear it, and let it settle: You are a priest for ever, on the word of Melchizedek, the king of righteousness.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the LORD swears, and God does not swear lightly. An oath is spoken once and cannot be unsaid. The Hebrew phrase 'will not relent' (lo yinachem) uses the verb that the KJV renders 'repent', which now sounds like guilt. The sense is that God will not change his mind. Meiri hears an echo of God 'regretting' Saul's kingship and says the oath is meant to set David's line apart. Make the pause before 'You' as long as the pause in verse 1: the speaker is looking directly at the one beside him.

The next words need care. 'Priest' (kohen) in the Hebrew Bible can also mean a royal minister or chief, as in 'David's sons were priests' (2 Sam 8:18), a text that Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak all cite. So the king may be called a priest in a sense wider than altar duty. The KJV's 'after the order of Melchizedek' hides the real Hebrew, 'al divrati malki-tzedeq', an uncommon phrase. Divrati has an extra yod. Rashi compares it with 'rabbati am' (Lam 1:1) and reads 'on the commission of Melchizedek', that is, in succession to him. Ibn Ezra offers several readings: a matter, a manner, or an abbreviated 'because you, like Melchizedek...'. Radak reads 'because you are a king of righteousness', splitting the name into its two words. The Targum goes this way too: 'because of the merit that you were a righteous king', said to the addressee himself. Malki-tzedeq means 'my king is righteous' or 'king of righteousness', a title in Jerusalem, whose king and priest he was in Genesis 14. Do not play 'order' as a guild. Play it as a title passed on to another: a person who takes up what that ancient king held.

philological_notes.note: Niphal of nacham: 'to relent, to change one's mind'. KJV 'repent' means this, not remorse for sin. Metzudat David glosses it as 'to turn back from his oath and think another thought'.
'Priest', but also a chief or minister: Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak all cite 'David's sons were priests' (2 Sam 8:18) to show that the word can mean ruler.

An uncommon form with an extra yod, meaning something like 'matter, manner, rank'. Rashi compares the yod with 'rabbati am' (Lam 1:1) and glosses 'on the commission of Melchizedek'. Metzudat Zion alone compares 'on the matter of the sons of men' (Eccl 3:18), with the yod superfluous. Ibn Ezra lists several possible senses.

The name means 'my king is righteous' or 'king of righteousness'. Radak and the Targum read it as two words said of the addressee: a righteous king. The Targum has 'because of the merit that you were a righteous king'.

verses.translation_literal: The Lord at your right hand has shattered kings on the day of his anger.
verses.translation_dramatic: The Lord stands at your right hand. And on the day his anger breaks, kings are shattered.
verses.directors_commentary:
The picture has turned over. In verse 1 the king sat at God's right hand; here the Lord is at the king's right hand, as his shield and champion. Hebrew does not hide the exchange, and it is a reminder that the positions are about nearness, not rank. The right hand was the sword hand; a soldier's right flank was covered by a comrade, and a defendant's advocate stood at his right (Psalm 109:31). Meiri compares: 'He stands at the right hand of the needy'. So God is both the king's guard and his weapon.

Here the Hebrew uses אֲדֹנָי, the divine title, a different form from the human 'my lord' (אֲדֹנִי) of verse 1. The KJV prints plain 'Lord' for both, so the English reader cannot tell the two apart; the Hebrew keeps them apart, and so should a reading.

The verb is מָחַץ, 'to smash, to shatter', the word for splitting a skull (Judges 5:26) and for God's wounding in Deuteronomy 32:39. The KJV's 'strike through' is mild; in the other English versions 'wound' is milder still. The Hebrew is perfect-tense, 'has shattered', and the commentators argue about it: Meiri calls it a past used for the future; Ibn Ezra reads it as a standing fact. 'The day of his anger' (יוֹם אַפּוֹ) is literally the day of his nose, as in the idiom, since the nostril flares. Keep the heat of it. Rashi finds in it Abraham's four kings; Malbim, David's capture of Rabbah. The actors do not need to choose: the voice is God's strength seen from the king's side.

philological_notes.note: 'Shatter, smash, pierce through', an act of violence on the body. Metzudat Zion: 'striking and wounding', as in Deuteronomy 32:39.
Literally 'his nose'; the nostril flares in anger, so 'anger' (KJV 'wrath'). The idiom is lost in English.

verses.translation_literal: He will judge among the nations; it is full of corpses; he has shattered a head over a great land.
verses.translation_dramatic: He will sit in judgment among the nations. And the ground is full, full of the dead. He has crushed the head of a great land.
verses.directors_commentary:
Three clauses, no connecting words, in the manner of a battlefield seen in a series of flashes. First, 'he judges among the nations': the verb דִּין is a courtroom word, and the point is that war here is a verdict, not a rampage. The KJV's 'heathen' for גּוֹיִם is a word loaded with later Christian meaning; the Hebrew simply says 'nations', and so the passage is about judgment on the world powers, not on religious outsiders.

Second, 'it is full of corpses' (מָלֵא גְוִיּוֹת). The subject is unstated, and the KJV supplies 'he shall fill the places', treating מָלֵא as a verb with an object. Rashi reads it differently: מָלֵא means 'a gathering' (as in Jeremiah 12:6, 'they cry aloud after you, a full company'), so it is a heap of bodies. The BBE adds 'valleys'. The Hebrew has only the bare fact. גְוִיָּה, 'corpse', is the same word used for bodies in Nahum 3:3. Do not soften it: this is a field of dead men.

Third, 'a head over a great land'. The singular רֹאשׁ may mean a single ruler: Rashi says Pharaoh, as in Habakkuk 3:13, 'you crushed the head of the house of the wicked'; Malbim says the capital, the head of the land. Or it is collective, 'heads', which is how the KJV and Radak read it ('over many countries'). Ibn Ezra reads the land as Israel, Media and Persia, or 'Rabbath of the Ammonites'. Either way, the director must decide whether the crushed head is a person or a place, and play it so.

philological_notes.note: Verb ('it is full') or noun ('a gathering, a full company'). Rashi compares Jeremiah 12:6 and Isaiah 31:4 for a noun meaning 'a full number'.
A head: a single ruler or heads collectively. Rashi: Pharaoh; Radak: 'a land of many heads, a general term'.

verses.translation_literal: From a wadi on the way he will drink; therefore he will lift up a head.
verses.translation_dramatic: He drinks from the stream beside the road, no halt, no feast, only a mouthful as he goes. And so, he lifts his head.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on its smallest image, and it is the one that makes the ending. A נַחַל is a wadi, a seasonal watercourse that is dry for most of the year and runs only in the rains; to find water in one 'on the way' is a traveller's luck. The warrior is on the march and does not stop; he stoops, drinks and goes on. This is the picture of a commander who does not rest until the work is finished, and it ties back to verse 1: the king who sits and waits will be the king who, when the time comes, drinks on the move.

The KJV 'brook' is soft and pastoral; the Hebrew wadi is a dry gully of the Judean wilderness, a sudden stream. Meiri and Radak read the drink as a figure of blood, 'the river ran with their blood' (compare Numbers 23:24, 'he drinks the blood of the slain'); Metzudat David reads it as sated with the blood of the slain. Rashi, following the other reading, makes the drinker Pharaoh or Sennacherib, who boasted of the river he drank from (Ezekiel 29:3; Isaiah 37:25). The text itself does not say, and an actor should keep the plain action.

The last word is the gesture: יָרִים רֹאשׁ, 'he lifts up the head', the opposite of the crushed head in verse 6. Heads fall and heads are raised; this is how the psalm closes. Ibn Ezra notes that the tenses change from perfect to imperfect and says there is no problem: Hebrew uses either for a standing truth.

philological_notes.note: From a wadi, a seasonal stream bed. Meiri and Radak take it as a river of blood, a figure of a great slaughter (compare Numbers 23:24).
'He lifts up the head', an idiom of triumph; Rashi says 'he was boasting of his greatness', Radak says 'he raised his head above all'. It answers the crushed head of verse 6.
